Learning Objectives
Discuss the indications and contraindications for conversion to total hip arthroplasty in the
setting of posttraumatic osteoarthritis.
Identify the various surgical challenges that entail posttraumatic hip osteoarthritis.
Perform an appropriate preoperative workup of and planning for patients requiring
conversion to total hip arthroplasty.
Review the complications and results of total hip arthroplasty for posttraumatic hip
osteoarthritis.

Posttraumatic hip osteoarthritis is a secondary osteoarthritis that may occur after trauma of
the hip joint involving the acetabulum, the proximal femur, or both. Surgical treatment options
for hip fractures generally are successful; however, postoperative complications commonly
occur.
Complications that may occur postoperatively include nonunion and malunion of the fracture,
hardware migration, femoral head osteonecrosis, infection, and posttraumatic osteoarthritis.
Failed surgical fixation of proximal femur fractures for any of these reasons often necessitates
conversion arthroplasty as subsequent surgical management.
Conversion total hip arthroplasty (THA) also is performed because of failed acetabular fracture
fixation, failed hemiarthroplasty, or after the development of posttraumatic osteoarthritis.
Epidemiology
Approximately 70% to 80% of THA procedures are performed for primary osteoarthritis;
however, the increasing incidence of fractures and osteoarthritis in the aging population may
contribute to rising numbers of conversion THA procedures currently performed in the United
States.
Posttraumatic osteoarthritis causes approximately 12% of all osteoarthritis cases.
Posttraumatic osteoarthritis may develop in 13% to 33% of patients with acetabular fractures
managed via open reduction and internal fixation,1 despite anatomic reduction.
After hip dislocation the incidence of posttraumatic osteoarthritis is 17% (anterior dislocation)
and 30% (posterior dislocation) if reduction takes place within 6 hours of dislocation, and 76%
if reduction is performed more than 6 hours postinjury.
The incidence of conversion THA after 5 years of first treatment is between 11% to 15%.
Anatomy and Biomechanics
A traumatic event may predispose a patient to hip osteoarthritis via direct cartilage injury or if
joint biomechanics are affected, leading to cartilage degeneration.

Anatomy and Biomechanics
Limited research is available on the pathomechanics of the disease, and different
theories exist with regard to how the injury leads to osteoarthritis. The injury may act as

the incipient lesion of osteoarthritis by altering the biomechanics across the joint if
malalignment, malorientation, and surface incongruities persist after repair. Irreversible
cartilage damage may occur at the time of impact, leading to chondrocyte death and
inflammation that ultimately results in osteoarthritis. Trabecular microfracture followed
by bone remodeling and damage to the surrounding musculature also may contribute to
posttraumatic osteoarthritis. The injury ultimately leads to biologic and mechanical
changes that destabilize the normal coupling of degeneration and synthesis of articular
cartilage, chondrocytes, extracellular matrix, and subchondral bone.
Etiology
Various reasons exist for conversion THA, including malunion, nonunion, implant failure or
cutout, soft-tissue irritation from hardware, femoral head osteonecrosis, and posttraumatic
arthritis (Table 1; Figure 1).

Natural History
Posttraumatic arthritis usually is associated with chronic pain, poor function, weakness, and
decreased quality of life.
Numerous surgical challenges are uniquely present in patients with arthritis secondary to
trauma with no primary osteoarthritis involvement, including concomitant infection,
neurologic impairment, joint stiffness, deformity, previous hardware, previous traumatic and
surgical wounds, bone loss, poor bone quality, and leg-length discrepancy.

The surgical outcomes of conversion THA are associated with higher incidence of serious
complications, including infection, intraoperative fractures, dislocation, loosening, heterotopic
ossification, muscle disruption and dysfunction, neurologic injury, and hematomas.
Patients who undergo conversion THA are more likely to require a revision procedure.
Risk Factors
Intra-articular injury and poor reduction after open reduction and internal fixation (>2 mm) is
associated with higher incidence of posttraumatic osteoarthritis (44%) (Video 1).
Delayed closed reduction (>6 hours) after traumatic hip dislocation
Younger patient age, the presence of sclerotic bone, abnormal anatomy after trauma, loss of
acetabular bone stock, and development of hardware complications are factors that lead to
higher revision rates after conversion THA.2


Risk Factors
In the setting of acetabular fractures, radiographic evaluation of the hip joint provides
information about the quality of fracture reduction. A meta-analysis conducted by
Giannoudis et al1 on surgical management for displaced acetabular fractures found that
despite satisfactory reduction (<2 mm) with open reduction and internal fixation, the
incidence of osteoarthritis was 13% (76 of 577 patients); however, if reduction was not
satisfactory (>2 mm), the incidence was markedly increased to 44% (47 of 108 patients).
In addition, Judet and cross-table lateral views may exclude any screw penetration into
the hip joint.
Classification
Posttraumatic osteoarthritis of the hip includes two main categories: prior acetabular trauma
and prior femoral trauma (femoral neck, intertrochanteric and pertrochanteric fractures;
Resource 1).
Other classification systems that are important to consider in the diagnosis and management of
posttraumatic hip osteoarthritis include:

Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History and Physical Examination
The initial evaluation begins with a thorough patient history and physical examination.
Determine previous fracture type and surgical procedures performed, as well as whether any
complications from prior procedures are present.
Specifically, inquire about postoperative infections and if any postoperative neurologic
complications may have improved.
A history of the patient’s functional status, activity level, and expectations also is useful for
counseling.

Patient History and Physical Examination

During the physical examination, the clinician should assess gait pattern, abductor
function, leg-length discrepancy, range of motion, rotational profile of the lower
extremity, previous incisions, muscle strength, and neurovascular status. Inspection of
incisions can establish the prior approach, soft-tissue quality, signs of chronic infection,
and the risk of subsequent wound healing complications.
Previous surgical notes and radiographs may provide useful information regarding the
prior approach, types of implants used, intraoperative complications, and abductor
muscle status. This information can help determine the appropriate surgical approach
for reconstruction and instruments that will facilitate implant removal.
Diagnostic Studies
Serum Laboratory Studies
Infectious laboratory studies (complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-
reactive protein level)4 are appropriate screening tools.
Hip Aspiration
Analysis of synovial fluid from the hip is important to rule out infection in patients in whom
strong clinical suspicion for infection exists.
Blood Cultures
Often negative but may be used to guide management of hematogenous osteomyelitis
Microbiology Studies
Sinus tract cultures
Not reliable for guiding antibiotic treatment5
Intraoperative tissue culture

Preferred method for guiding antibiotic treatment

Diagnostic Studies
Active infection is an absolute contraindication to THA and must be excluded
preoperatively. Hip infection should be considered in patients with unexplained levels of
pain, a history of wound problems, or radiographic evidence of a possible infection.
Complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein level are
effective preoperative screening tools; however, occult infections may still be missed.
Patients with borderline or elevated inflammatory markers should increase suspicion for
infection, and analysis of synovial fluid of the hip should be performed. If an active
infection is confirmed, surgical management should proceed in a staged fashion. A two-
stage protocol includes implant removal, meticulous débridement, and resection
arthroplasty or placement of an antibiotic-loaded cement spacer. Definitive
reconstruction may be performed later if infection is eradicated. Obtaining
intraoperative cultures routinely is recommended in patients with prior implants, even if
preoperative infectious workup is negative because occult infections can occur.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Preoperative radiographic evaluation includes an AP view of the pelvis, and AP and lateral
views of the affected hip.
Judet views are helpful in patients with a previous acetabular fracture to evaluate the integrity
of the anterior and posterior columns.
Full-length femur views should be obtained in patients with a previous femoral fracture to
assess deformities and the distal extent of retained implants.

Radiography

Plain radiographs are the best initial imaging study for useful and extensive information
for diagnostic purposes (disease severity, bone loss, leg-length discrepancies,
deformities, heterotopic ossification), and for preoperative planning (previous hardware
characteristics, digital templating, femoral offset, approach selection). Existing implants
can be evaluated to determine if they are well fixed or loose and if removal is necessary
for proper implant positioning. Acetabular and femoral bone deficiencies can be
assessed and classified according to the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons or
Paprosky classification systems.
Computed Tomography
CT aids in diagnosis and surgical planning.
Sensitivity and specificity may be affected by hardware artifact.

Computed Tomography
CT with three-dimensional reconstructions can provide additional information in
patients with severe bone deficiencies, extensive heterotopic ossification, intra-articular
hardware (Figure 3), or acetabular deformities and about the fracture healing process
(suspected nonunion), integrity of the columns, or torsional deformities of the proximal
femur that cannot be adequately assessed on radiographs. Currently, three-dimensional
printed models may be used to better understand a complex malunion to plan the best
acetabular reconstruction.

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Best imaging modality for diagnosing chronic osteomyelitis and localizing infection
T2-weighted sequences will show bone and soft-tissue edema.
Penumbra sign (T1-weighted sequences: dark central abscess with bright internal wall and
dark external sclerotic rim)
Sensitivity and specificity: if negative, rules out osteomyelitis; if positive, may overestimate the
extent of osteomyelitis.

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
The role of MRI is limited if previous hardware is present; however, valuable information
is obtained regarding staged reconstructions performed because of concerns for
infection (chronic osteomyelitis or septic nonunion) and after hardware is removed. MRI
may demonstrate sequestrum and involucrum, aid in diagnosis and surgical planning. In
those patients, an antibiotic-loaded hip articulating spacer in combination with

Total joint arthroplasty in patients with posttraumatic arthritis of the hip is associated
with higher risks for surgical site infections or periprosthetic joint infections. The
incidence is markedly higher in patients who have undergone previous surgical
procedures and have retained implants.6
Bone Scintigraphy
Minimal role in posttraumatic osteoarthritis; highly sensitive but not specific
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Indications
First-line treatment for the management of posttraumatic osteoarthritis of the hip
Involves a sequence of nonpharmacologic therapies followed by pharmacologic options aimed
at relieving pain and improving function
Patients with severe medical conditions precluding any surgical treatment
Contraindications
No response to a trial of nonpharmacologic and pharmacologic options with advanced
structural hip osteoarticular disease and substantial symptoms affecting patient quality of life
Concomitant infection requiring surgical and antibiotic treatment
Techniques/Procedures
Nonpharmacologic Measures
Physical therapy and exercises, weight management, walking aids, lifestyle modifications
Pharmacologic Measures
Acetaminophen, NSAIDs (oral and topical), and intra-articular glucocorticoid injections


Nonsurgical Management
Similar to other arthritic conditions, early management of posttraumatic hip
osteoarthritis begins with nonsurgical management. Some lifestyle modifications
minimizing the stress and articular impact may protect the affected hip joint and slow
the progress of osteoarthritis. Specific exercises may help increase range of motion and
flexibility and strengthen the muscles in the hip and leg. The use of NSAIDs in most
patients is limited by the increased risk of serious gastrointestinal, cardiovascular, and
renal complications. In patients with comorbidities, such as diabetes mellitus,
hypertension, and advanced age, a cyclooxygenase-2 selective NSAID or a nonselective
NSAID should be used in combination with a proton-pump inhibitor; however, use of
these medications in patients with a high comorbidity risk is not preferred (eg, previous
gastrointestinal bleeding or chronic renal failure). Intra-articular cortisone injections into
the painful joint may afford temporary pain relief and may help differentiate other
sources of pain.
Surgical Management
Indications
Indications for conversion to THA in patients with prior trauma are similar to those for primary
osteoarthritis.
These include severe debilitating pain that affects quality of life and activities of daily living and
failed nonsurgical management. In addition to pain, a severe limp or leg-length discrepancy
causing notable functional limitations also may be an indication for surgical management.
Key elements of surgical management include removal of hardware interfering with the THA
implant, restoration of hip biomechanics, and minimization of intraoperative and
postoperative complications (Videos 2 and 3).

Contraindications
Absolute contraindications include active infection and notable medical conditions that
increase a patient’s risk of morbidity or mortality.
Conversion THA is associated with greater morbidity than primary THA, and the clinician
should assess whether any medical conditions, such as glycemic control, tobacco use, and
anemia, can be optimized preoperatively.
In younger patients (45 years or younger) special consideration should be given to whether the
native hip can be preserved via any nonarthroplasty options. For patients with a viable femoral
head and intact joint space, revision fracture fixation or osteotomy may be preferred.
Techniques/Procedures
Preoperative Planning
Digital templating is critical to preoperative planning to select the implant that restores the
anatomy of the affected hip in terms of sizing, geometry, center of rotation, offset, and leg
length.
Aids in determining whether intraoperative imaging will be helpful for hardware removal or
implant placement
Must follow the mnemonic ABCDE of the preoperative principles for complex arthroplasty
reconstruction (Figure 4):
A, approach: recognition of previous approaches or surgical incisions
B, bone loss: assessment of acetabular or femoral bone loss to anticipate the various surgical
treatment options and equipment to manage the situation (eg, bone grafting, cup-cages,
distal fixation femoral stems, proximal femur replacement)
C, constraint level: determine the constraint level necessary to minimize hip instability (large
femoral head, dual-mobility cups, offset or constrained liners)
D, deformity: proximal femur malunion fractures are associated with deformities that may
require consideration in terms of surgical approach (trochanteric osteotomies) and implant
morphology selection
E, extraction equipment: if existing hardware is expected to be removed because of
interference with arthroplasty reconstruction, surgeons must anticipate the need for special

Surgical Approaches
Surgical approach to the hip (including the direct anterior, anterolateral, and posterior
approach) depends on the exposure necessary based on the situation and surgeon
preference.

Prior surgical incisions are incorporated if they do not compromise exposure, and the
approach is extended as necessary.
Multiples approaches may be necessary to remove hardware from the acetabulum and femur.
In situ femoral neck osteotomy should be considered in patients with ankylosis.

Surgical Approaches
In patients with a history of posterior column fixation or notable acetabular deformity, a
posterior approach offers the most extensile acetabular exposure. Surgeon should give
special surgical consideration to the posterior capsule, which is taken down as a sleeve,
tagged, and repaired at the end of the procedure to enhance postoperative stability. In
addition, care is taken to protect the sciatic nerve throughout the procedure.
For isolated anterior column fixation or femoral implants, an anterolateral approach may
be preferred, depending on surgeon familiarity. This approach may enhance
postoperative stability by preserving the posterior structures and is easily extended
along the femoral shaft. The anterolateral approach also decreases the risk of direct
injury to the sciatic nerve. In selected patients in whom the surgeon plans to retain
previous implants, the direct anterior approach also may be considered.
In patients with ankylosis, the femoral neck may be osteotomized in situ or constrictive
osteophytes may be removed before hip dislocation to prevent iatrogenic fractures.
Patients with femoral neck hardware should undergo a hip dislocation before implant
removal to prevent fractures.
In patients with a history of acetabular trauma, special care is taken during reaming
because the bone quality usually is poor from disuse osteopenia. Prior fixation implants
are selectively removed as necessary. Posterior column screws often are encountered
during reaming, and these screws may be removed if easily accessible or burred away
from inside to allow for proper acetabular component seating. Bone defects may be
grafted with the use of femoral head autograft or allograft, and reverse reaming is
performed to compact the bone graft into place. After adequate reamer engagement is
observed, a trial implant is used to assess stability of rim fit. Cementless, highly porous-

including augments and cages. If possible, larger inner-diameter highly cross-linked
polyethylene liner options or dual-mobility constructs are used to optimize stability and
minimize hip dislocations.
Patient Positioning
Patient positioning depends on the surgical approach.
Lateral decubitus position for posterior and anterolateral approaches; supine position for
direct anterior approach.
A radiolucent table can be used to facilitate intraoperative imaging for hardware extraction
and implant positioning.

Patient Positioning
Patient positioning is based on the selected surgical approach. Patients undergoing
anterior approaches are placed in the supine position, whereas patients undergoing
posterior approaches are placed in the lateral decubitus position with the surgical side
up. The use of a radiolucent table and imaging via C-arm or traditional flat plate
radiographs allows for intraoperative localization of hardware to facilitate extraction; this
is particularly useful to remove deep acetabular screws or locking femoral nail screws.
The direct anterior approach can be performed on a standard table or traction table.
Serious complications related to surgical positioning on a traction table are relatively
uncommon; however, if a traction table is used, care must be taken to avoid creating a
fracture of the ankle or tibia with the traction boot device and to avoid iatrogenic
proximal femur fracture from excessive force application with the hydraulic hook device.
Postoperative Management
Weight-bearing status depends on specific circumstances; however, weight bearing as
tolerated is desirable.

Early mobilization to reduce complications
Mechanical and pharmacologic venous thromboembolism prophylaxis is recommended per
institutional protocols.7
Antibiotic agents are routinely administered within 1 hour before incision and continued for 24
hours postoperatively.
Routine drain use is controversial.
Closed incisional negative-pressure wound therapy may be considered to promote healing and
avoid postoperative hematoma.

Postoperative Management
One of the main goals of postoperative management is early mobilization to reduce
complications associated with prolonged recumbency, such as atelectasis, pulmonary
infection, and venous thromboembolic events. For prior acetabular trauma, weight
bearing is restricted postoperatively if notable bone grafting is performed or if initial
implant stability relies markedly on screw fixation. Patients are instructed to remain toe-
touch weight bearing for 6 to 12 weeks postoperatively until stable bone ingrowth is
observed. In patients with prior femoral trauma, weight-bearing status is determined by
the presence of a trochanteric osteotomy or bone defects. In the absence of an
osteotomy or notable defects, weight bearing as tolerated may be initiated. Conversely,
if a trochanteric osteotomy is performed, toe-touch weight bearing is initiated for 6
weeks postoperatively. At that time, weight bearing can be progressed if no migration of
the trochanteric fragment or implants is observed. Because all cases of complex hip
arthroplasty are associated with a higher risk of instability, surgeons should be
conservative in instituting hip precautions for most patients. The exact degree of activity
restriction and the duration of precautions vary depending on the complexity of prior
injury, abductor mechanism integrity, and the surgical approach used. A deep drain may
be placed if extensive soft-tissue dissection and dead space are present, especially in the
setting of therapeutic-level anticoagulation postoperatively. Closed incisional negative-
pressure wound therapy works via the mechanisms of microdeformation and
macrodeformation. Fluid removal stabilizes the wound environment, resulting in less
tissue edema, decreased wound healing time, and improved skin graft survival. Recent
studies have demonstrated that high-risk patients may benefit from closed incisional

Complications
Conversion to THA is associated with a high incidence of intraoperative and postoperative
complications (overall complication rate, 10.2%).
Complications can be minimized via a thorough preoperative evaluation.
Heterotopic ossification is the most common complication (30%), followed by infection (6%),
dislocation (4%), and nerve injuries (2%).

Complications
Intraoperative complications include prolonged surgical time (range, 97 to 240 min),
blood loss (800 to 1000 mL), sciatic nerve injury (2.7%), and intraoperative fractures.
Postoperative complications include infection (2% to 10.2%), dislocation (3% to 6%), leg-
length discrepancy, weakness (abductor insufficiency), heterotopic ossification (30% to
43%), and loosening (as high as 20%).
Arthroplasty for posttraumatic osteoarthritis is associated with greater intraoperative
blood loss than routine primary hip arthroplasty. One measure to decrease
intraoperative blood loss is the use of antifibrinolytic agents, such as tranexamic acid. If
estimated blood loss is likely to be high, intraoperative cell salvage systems should be
available. This allows for the transfusion of autologous blood and decreases the risk for
needing postoperative allogeneic blood transfusion. To prevent sciatic nerve injury and
reduce surgical time, meticulous preoperative planning is necessary to anticipate the
best surgical approach to attain adequate and extensile exposure.
Surgical site infection and periprosthetic joint infection are devastating complications
after conversion to THA; special attention should be paid to American Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons clinical practice guidelines for prophylactic antibiotic use and

antiseptic use. Other intraoperative adjuvants include the use of diluted betadine9
(0.35% povidone-iodine) or chlorhexidine gluconate (0.05%) lavage for 3 minutes before
wound closure. Extended postoperative antibiotic prophylaxis protocol for 10 days may
be recommended in select patients at high risk for infection. These protocols have been
associated with a statistically significant and clinically meaningful reduction in the 90-day
infection rate.10
If heterotopic bone is removed during THA, perioperative low-dose radiation therapy or
postoperative management via NSAIDs (indomethacin) should be considered to
minimize the risk for recurrent heterotopic bone formation after THA. If possible, larger
inner-diameter highly cross-linked polyethylene liner options or dual-mobility constructs
are used to optimize stability and minimize hip dislocations in combination with
approach-specific hip precautions and restrictions for at least 6 weeks postoperatively.
Outcomes
Conversion to THA for posttraumatic arthritis is associated with favorable improvements in
pain and function.
Results of conversion to THA after posttraumatic osteoarthritis generally are less favorable
than those of THA for primary osteoarthritis and are associated with higher revision rates (3%
to 43%).
Careful patient selection, thorough preoperative planning, meticulous surgical execution, and
early postoperative mobilization can optimize outcomes while minimizing complications.

Outcomes
Patients seeking conversion THA after prior acetabular trauma generally are younger
than patients undergoing THA for primary hip osteoarthritis. Conversely, patients
requiring conversion THA after prior proximal femur trauma are older and less active
than those undergoing hip arthroplasty for primary osteoarthritis; age and functional
status are important factors that affect outcomes. A systematic review by Schwarzkopf et

Conversion to THA in patients with posttraumatic osteoarthritis includes a wide
spectrum of conditions, from prior cannulated screw fixation for femoral neck fractures
to complex posttraumatic acetabular or femoral deformities. Therefore, the reported
outcomes vary depending on the trauma type and fixation performed. For example,
